title: Daily returns
code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([100, 110, 99])
print(s.pct_change().round(2).tolist())
why: pct_change divides each price by the one before: 110/100 − 1 = 0.1, 99/110 − 1 = −0.1. The first has nothing before it, so it is NaN, not 0.

title: Shifting a series
code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(s.shift(1).tolist())
why: shift(1) moves values down a row, so each row sees yesterday's value. That's how you lag a signal so it only uses past data. The gap becomes NaN, and the integers turn into floats to hold it.

title: A rolling mean
code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([2, 4, 6, 8])
print(s.rolling(3).mean().tolist())
why: A 3-row window needs three values, so the first two rows are NaN. Then (2+4+6)/3 = 4 and (4+6+8)/3 = 6.

title: Log returns
code:
import numpy as np
p = np.array([100.0, 120.0, 100.0])
r = np.diff(np.log(p))
print(round(r.sum(), 4))
why: Log returns add up: log(120/100) + log(100/120) = log(100/100) = 0. Simple returns don't: +20% then −16.7% sums to +3.3% though the price ended where it started.

title: Compounding
code:
import pandas as pd
r = pd.Series([0.10, -0.10])
print(round((1 + r).prod() - 1, 4))
why: Up 10% then down 10%: 1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99, a 1% loss. Returns compound by multiplying, which is why a loss needs a bigger gain to recover.

title: Sample or population
code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
x = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(round(x.std(), 3), round(np.std(x.values), 3))
why: pandas' std divides by n − 1 (the sample standard deviation); NumPy's divides by n unless you pass ddof=1. Mixing them gives different vols from the same data.

title: Annualising vol
code:
import numpy as np
daily = 0.01
print(round(daily * np.sqrt(252), 3))
why: Volatility scales with the square root of time: 1% × √252 ≈ 15.9%. Multiplying by 252 is the classic mistake.

title: Maximum drawdown
code:
import pandas as pd
eq = pd.Series([100, 120, 90, 110, 80])
dd = eq / eq.cummax() - 1
print(round(dd.min(), 3))
why: The running peak reaches 120. The worst point after it is 80: 80/120 − 1 = −33.3%. Drawdown is measured from the peak, not from the start.

title: Grouping by sector
code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'sector': ['IT', 'IT', 'Bank'], 'ret': [0.02, 0.04, -0.01]})
print(df.groupby('sector')['ret'].mean().round(2).to_dict())
why: groupby averages each sector on its own: IT (0.02 + 0.04)/2 = 0.03. Groups come out sorted by key, so Bank comes first.

title: Boolean masks
code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([3, -1, 2, -4])
print(s[s > 0].sum(), (s > 0).mean())
why: s[s > 0] keeps 3 and 2, which sum to 5. (s > 0) is True, False, True, False, and the mean of booleans is the share that's True: a hit rate of 0.5.

title: Merging tables
code:
import pandas as pd
a = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2, 3]})
b = pd.DataFrame({'id': [2, 3, 4], 'px': [10, 20, 30]})
print(len(a.merge(b, on='id')), len(a.merge(b, on='id', how='left')))
why: An inner merge keeps ids in both tables (2 and 3). A left merge keeps every row of a, with NaN where b has no match. Silent row loss in merges is a common backtest bug.

title: Ranking
code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([0.05, -0.02, 0.01])
print(s.rank().tolist())
why: rank() gives 1 to the smallest value by default, so 0.05 is 3rd of 3. Cross-sectional signals are often ranked like this before building a long-short book.

title: Correlation
code:
import pandas as pd
x = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(round(x.corr(-2 * x + 5), 2))
why: y = −2x + 5 is a straight line sloping down, so the correlation is exactly −1. Correlation ignores scale and shift; it can't be −2.

title: Portfolio return
code:
import numpy as np
w = np.array([0.5, 0.3, 0.2])
r = np.array([0.02, -0.01, 0.05])
print(round(w @ r, 4))

title: Floor division
why: // rounds down toward minus infinity, not toward zero, so −7 // 2 is −4. It bites when bucketing negative numbers.

title: Two names, one list
code:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)
why: b = a doesn't copy: both names point to the same list. Use a.copy() when you want a separate one, or a DataFrame changed in one place changes everywhere.

title: Filling gaps
code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([100, None, None, 103])
print(s.ffill().tolist())
why: ffill carries the last known value forward, which is safe for prices. bfill (the last option) would copy a future price backwards: look-ahead.

title: Missing values
code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([1, None, 3])
print(s.mean(), len(s), s.count())
options: nan 3 2
why: mean skips NaN by default: (1 + 3)/2 = 2. len counts rows, count counts non-missing values. A gap in data quietly changes your averages.

title: Sorting
code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'d': [3, 1, 2], 'px': [30, 10, 20]})
df.sort_values('d')
print(df['px'].tolist())
options: None
why: sort_values returns a new DataFrame; it doesn't change df. Without df = df.sort_values('d'), returns would be computed on unsorted dates.

title: A trend signal
code:
df['ma'] = df['close'].rolling(20).mean()
df['signal'] = (df['close'] > df['ma']).astype(int)
df['pnl'] = df['signal'] * df['close'].pct_change()
options: The signal uses today's close but earns today's return: shift it a day
rolling(20) leaves out today's close, so the average is a day stale
pct_change compounds wrongly here, so it should use log returns instead
astype(int) turns every short signal into a zero, so it never shorts
why: Today's signal is set at the close, so it can only earn tomorrow's return. Multiplying by today's return trades on information you didn't have: look-ahead. df['signal'].shift(1) fixes it.

title: Building the universe
code:
universe = nifty50_members(date='today')
prices = load_prices(universe, start='2010-01-01')
result = backtest(prices)
options: It only tests today's index members, missing stocks that dropped out since 2010
start is passed as a string, so the prices load from the wrong year by default
Fifty stocks are too few to backtest, so the result can't be trusted at all
It loads prices when a backtest needs returns, so every number is off by one
why: Today's index members are the survivors. Stocks that fell out of the index since 2010, often after big losses, are missing, so the backtest looks better than reality. Use the members as of each date.

title: Annualising Sharpe
code:
daily = strategy_returns
sharpe = daily.mean() / daily.std() * 252
options: It should multiply by the square root of 252, not 252
It should divide by 252
It should use the median instead of the mean
std should be replaced by variance
why: Mean returns scale with time, volatility with its square root, so the Sharpe ratio scales by √252 ≈ 15.9. Multiplying by 252 inflates it about 16 times.

title: Normalising a signal
code:
z = (x - x.mean()) / x.std()
df['signal'] = z > 2
options: The mean and std are taken over all data, future included
z > 2 misses the days where z is exactly two, so use >=
x.std() divides by n − 1, so the z-scores are too small
A z-score can't be a signal unless it is ranked first
why: Each day's z-score uses a mean and a standard deviation computed over all data, future included. Use a rolling or expanding window so each day only sees its past.

title: Training a model
code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3)
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
options: The split is random, so it trains on days after the ones it tests on
A test size of 0.3 is too big for time series, so it should be 0.2
The model is fit before scaling, so the features are on different scales
y_tr and y_te are in the wrong order, so the labels are swapped round
why: train_test_split shuffles by default. With time series, nearby days are related, so training on later and neighbouring days leaks information into the test. Split by date (or shuffle=False), and purge overlaps.

title: Returns from raw prices
code:
raw = load_close(symbol, adjusted=False)
ret = raw.pct_change()
print(ret.min())
options: A 1:2 split shows as a −50% return; use split-adjusted prices
pct_change can't handle the first row, so min() returns NaN
min() finds the best day here; the worst day needs max()
Returns must be in percent before min() can compare them
why: Unadjusted prices drop on splits and bonus issues even though holders lose nothing. Returns from them show fake crashes. Use prices adjusted for corporate actions.

title: Total return
code:
total = daily_returns.sum()
print(f'Total return: {total:.1%}')
options: Simple returns compound, so total is (1 + r).prod() − 1
It should take the mean of returns, not their sum, for a total
The f-string rounds to one decimal, so the total is off by 10%
The first day has no return, so the sum is short by a day
why: Summing simple returns ignores compounding; over long or volatile periods the gap is large. Multiply the growth factors, or sum log returns and convert back.

title: Joining fundamentals
code:
df = prices.merge(earnings, left_on='date', right_on='quarter_end')
df['eps'] = df['eps'].ffill()
options: EPS is joined on quarter end, weeks before results were out
ffill copies EPS backwards in time; it should be bfill
An inner merge drops days, so it needs how='outer' to work
EPS is in rupees per share but prices are in crores here
why: Results come out weeks after the quarter ends. Joining on quarter end lets the backtest use EPS before anyone knew it. Join on the announcement date: point-in-time data.

title: Net returns
code:
trades = df['position'].diff().abs()
df['net'] = df['gross'] - 0.0005
print(df['net'].mean())
options: It charges costs every day, not per trade: trades is never used
diff() should be pct_change(), or position changes are wrong
0.0005 is 5%, not 5 bps, so the cost is a hundred times too big
abs() makes sells count as buys, so costs are counted twice
why: Costs are paid when you trade. It should be df['gross'] - trades * 0.0005. As written, a fund that never trades pays costs and a busy one pays too little.
